 Enable camera-side motion detection and set detect.motion: true per camera 
 Field Notes and Lessons Learned
 Windows is not required. Frigate + Linux handles Reolink, Hikvision, Dahua, Amcrest, and ONVIF RTSP streams reliably. Blue Iris is only justified when the user insists on Windows or needs its proprietary camera integrations.
 Coral over GPU for AI. Field testing confirms Coral handles 15+ camera streams and ~100 FPS inference at <5 W, while a Tesla P4 idle draws 80 W with constant thermal load. Coral is the correct tool for sub-30-camera installs.
 iGPU beats discrete GPU for Plex alone. Unless transcode count exceeds iGPU ceiling (2–3 for UHD 530, 4–6 for UHD 770), a discrete GPU adds cost and noise with no benefit. Add discrete GPU only when ≥6 concurrent 4K transcodes are required.
 Skip the X99 unless growth is planned. The X99 platform excels at headroom but adds noise, heat, and power draw. A refurbished Dell Optiplex with i7-6700 + 32 GB RAM + 4-bay enclosure hits the 80% of requirements at 30% of the cost.
 Hyperconverged ≠ fragile. Plex on /dev/dri in LXC and Frigate on Coral in LXC are isolated by cgroup and namespace. A Frigate crash does not affect Plex; a Plex transcode storm does not starve Coral inference.
 Backup before going live. Configure vzdump weekly + ZFS snapshot replication to a second pool or offsite. NVR footage is irreplaceable; Plex metadata rebuild is annoying but tractable.
 FAQ
 Can Plex and the NVR share the same Coral TPU?
 No—Coral is a single-purpose inference accelerator, not a shared GPU. Run Coral only with Frigate (or another AI detector). Plex hardware transcoding requires Quick Sync, NVENC, or Intel Arc; assign the iGPU or discrete GPU to Plex exclusively. Both can coexist in the same host if the Coral is passed to the Frigate LXC and the iGPU is mounted in the Plex LXC.
 How much storage do I need for 8 cameras at 30-day retention?
 For 8 cameras at 4 Mbps H.265, 24/7 recording, allocate approximately 10.4 TB raw. Add 30–50% overhead for motion gaps, Frigate clip retention, and Plex media. A 4-bay chassis with 4× 8 TB drives in RAIDZ2 yields 16 TB usable, which is sufficient for the 8-camera install plus several TB of Plex media.
 Do I need Plex Pass for hardware transcoding?
 Yes. Plex disables hardware acceleration (Quick Sync, NVENC, Arc, AMF) without an active Plex Pass subscription. Software transcoding on CPU alone caps at 1–2 simultaneous 1080p sessions even on an i7-6700. Budget the Plex Pass (lifetime or annual) as a mandatory component.
 Is Proxmox or Synology DSM the right choice for a non-Linux user?
 Synology DSM is the right choice for users who prefer a GUI-driven, appliance-style experience and accept its limitations (no Coral, no discrete GPU, 6 GB RAM ceiling, 4 bays max). Proxmox is the right choice for users willing to learn Linux basics and who anticipate adding services (Home Assistant, game servers, AD/DC, web hosting). Both are stable; the deciding factor is growth intent and Linux comfort.
 What is the minimum iGPU generation for 4K HDR Plex tone-mapping?
 Intel 7th gen (Kaby Lake) UHD 630 is the practical floor for HEVC HDR→SDR tone-mapping. The 6th gen UHD 530 handles 4K HEVC decode but tone-mapping is limited and may fall back to software on certain clients. For reliable 4K HDR transcode with tone-mapping, target 8th gen or newer, or use Intel Arc A310/A380 which handles tone-mapping without CPU fallback.

Frigate NVR on a Raspberry Pi 5 With a Coral TPU 
 Skip to content 
 Frigate NVR on a Raspberry Pi 5 With a Coral TPU
 September 11, 2026 
 Jonathan Mitchell 
 Hardware hacking · raspberry pi 
 The one piece missing from this blog’s Pi 5 home server stack
 Between Pi-hole, Home Assistant, Ollama, Vaultwarden with Tailscale, and now Immich, this blog has built out most of a proper 2026 Raspberry Pi 5 home server. The piece still missing is video: turning cheap RTSP security cameras into a real, self-hosted NVR with object detection – without the CPU load that normally makes that impossible on a Pi. Running Frigate NVR on a Raspberry Pi 5 with a Coral Edge TPU is exactly how to fill that gap.
 Why a Coral TPU, not just the Pi’s own CPU
 Running object detection on every frame of every camera stream would pin a Pi 5’s CPU instantly. The Coral Edge TPU offloads that inference to dedicated silicon, so Frigate can run continuous, multi-camera object detection – people, vehicles, animals – at a fraction of the CPU cost of software-only detection.
 USB Coral Accelerator – simplest setup, no extra drivers beyond libedgetpu1-std , plugs into a Pi 5’s USB 3.0 port
 PCIe Coral (via M.2/HAT) – marginally better throughput, worth it only if you’re already running an NVMe HAT with a spare M.2 slot
 Either option is enough for several 1080p RTSP streams with detection latency low enough to be genuinely useful for alerts
 The basic setup
 Frigate ships as a Docker image, which is the officially recommended way to run it – there’s no case for compiling it from source on a Pi.
 Install Docker on Raspberry Pi OS (64-bit is required) if it isn’t already part of your Pi 5 stack
 Install libedgetpu1-std on the host and pass the Coral device through to the container
 Point Frigate’s config at each camera’s RTSP stream and set the detector to use the Coral TPU rather than CPU
 Store recordings on an NVMe SSD rather than the SD card – continuous recording will wear out an SD card fast
 A minimal detector config in config.yml looks like this:
 detectors: coral: {type: edgetpu, device: usb} 
 Fitting it into the rest of the stack
 Frigate’s real value on a home-server Pi comes from what it connects to, not from running in isolation:
 Home Assistant integration – Frigate’s HACS integration surfaces per-camera person/vehicle detection as sensors you can build automations around
 Immich – keep Frigate’s job strictly to live monitoring and alerts, and let Immich remain your actual photo/video library, rather than duplicating storage between the two
 Tailscale – expose Frigate’s web UI over your existing Tailscale network instead of opening another port to the internet
 Common gotchas worth knowing before you start
 Frigate needs a 64-bit OS – if you’re still running a 32-bit Raspberry Pi OS image from an older Pi 4 setup, you’ll need to reflash before any of this works
 The USB Coral Accelerator can run warm under sustained load – a small heatsink or a case with airflow is worth adding if it’s running continuously rather than just for testing
 RTSP camera firmware varies wildly in stream quality reporting – test with a short sub-stream resolution first rather than assuming your cameras’ main stream is what you actually want Frigate detecting against
 What to expect realistically
 A single Pi 5 with a Coral TPU handles a handful of cameras comfortably – this isn’t a replacement for a dedicated NVR box watching twenty cameras across a commercial site. For a home setup of two to six cameras, though, it’s a genuinely capable, low-power, fully self-hosted alternative to a cloud camera subscription, and it slots into a Pi 5 home-lab stack you may well already be running for everything else.
